title: How can one seed grow an entire wallet?
dek: One backup, billions of keys. The trick is a 32-byte companion to every key, and a rule about which branches an extended public key may follow.

blocks.text: When BIP 32 was written, the reference wallet generated each key at random. To avoid needing a new backup after every transaction, it kept a pool of a hundred spare keys. Every key was independent, so every key had to be saved.

BIP 32, assigned in 2012 and recorded as deployed, takes another route: derive every key from one seed, arranged as a tree. Branches of that tree can be shared with other systems, entirely or in part, with or without the ability to spend.

figure.title: The first split
figure.caption: HMAC-SHA512 turns a seed into 64 bytes. The left half becomes the master private key; the right half becomes the master chain code.

blocks.text: Every node in the tree is an *extended key*: an ordinary key plus a chain code, 32 more bytes of entropy. BIP 32 adds the chain code so that a node’s children do not depend on the key alone. The chain code is the same in the private and the public version of a node.
An ordinary public key cannot reveal its children. To derive them, you also need the chain code: together they form the extended public key.

An extended private key is the pair (k, c): private key and chain code. Its public counterpart is (K, c), where K is the public key for k. Turning the first into the second is called neutering it, because the result can no longer sign transactions.

blocks.title: Key plus chain code
blocks.caption: An extended key is a key and a chain code. Neutering swaps the private key for its public key and keeps the very same chain code.

blocks.text: To make child number *i*, run HMAC-SHA512 keyed with the parent’s chain code. The 64-byte output splits as the master did. The left half is added to the parent’s private key, modulo the order of the curve, to give the child’s private key. The right half becomes the child’s chain code.

What goes into the HMAC depends on the index. Indices 0 to 2³¹ − 1 are *normal*, and the input is the parent’s public key followed by the index. Indices from 2³¹ upward are *hardened*, and the input is the parent’s private key, padded with a zero byte, followed by the index. Paths mark hardened indices with an H: `m/0H/1` is normal child 1 of hardened child 0 of the master.

blocks.title: What goes into the HMAC
blocks.caption: The same 37 bytes of HMAC data, filled two ways. A normal child hashes the parent’s public key; a hardened child hashes its private key, padded with a zero byte.

blocks.text: In rare cases a step produces an invalid key, and the wallet moves on to the next index. BIP 32 puts the odds below one in 2¹²⁷. That one difference in the HMAC input, public key or private key, is what the figure below is about.

blocks.title: Who can derive what
blocks.caption: A hardened edge is a wall for public keys. Holding M, you can follow normal edges down to M/1/0, but you cannot cross into m/0H: deriving it needs a private key you do not have.

sections.heading: What an extended public key can do

blocks.text: Because a normal child’s HMAC input is the parent’s public key, someone holding only the extended public key can compute the child’s public key and chain code too: add the public point of the left half to the parent’s public key. BIP 32 notes that both routes give the same child, and that this is exactly what makes normal keys useful.

blocks.title: Two routes, one child
blocks.caption: Two ways to the same child public key. Only the left one needs the private key; the build checks that both agree for every normal child in the tree.

blocks.text: Its own example is a webshop. The shop’s server can hold one extended public key and generate a fresh address for every order, without ever holding a key that could spend the payments. Disclosure of that xpub alone reveals incoming payments but does not enable spending the wallet’s existing outputs. Our operational caution is that control of the server can still let an attacker replace the receiving addresses it displays and divert future payments, without deriving a private key.

BIP 32 lists other kinds of partial sharing too. An auditor can be given every account’s extended public key and see all transactions without a single secret key. A business partner can be given one account’s external chain and use it as a kind of super address, without asking for a new address for each payment.

blocks.title: Sharing without spending
blocks.caption: BIP 32’s examples of sharing part of a wallet. Each party holds an extended public key; none of them holds a key that can spend.

blocks.text: Hardened children are different. Their HMAC input contains the parent’s private key, so public derivation is simply not defined for them, and there is no way at all from a public parent to a private child. An extended public key reaches the public keys of descendants that are linked to it by normal steps only, and nothing else.

If normal derivation is so useful, why not use it everywhere? BIP 32 points to a weakness that is easy to miss. An extended public key, together with the private key of any descendant reached from it by normal steps only, is equivalent to the parent’s extended private key, and therefore to every key beneath it.

For a normal child, the parent xpub reveals the HMAC value added during derivation. Anyone who also obtains that child’s private key can subtract the value again to recover the parent’s private key. The example below shows the recovery on BIP 32’s published vector.

blocks.title: An xpub plus one leaked key
blocks.caption: BIP 32’s warning, recomputed on the published vector. A leaked child key and its parent’s xpub give back the parent’s private key; the hardened edge above the parent stops the climb there.

blocks.text: This is why BIP 32 uses hardened derivation at the account level. A leak of one account’s private keys then cannot climb past the hardened edge to the master or to other accounts. It is also why BIP 32 says extended public keys must be treated more carefully than ordinary public keys. The risk to funds arises only when an extended public key meets a leaked private key reached from it by normal steps; on its own it reconstructs public keys and nothing more.

blocks.label: Caveat
blocks.text: Sharing an extended public key is also a privacy decision. It lets the holder see every public key reached from it by normal steps, and with them the payments. BIP 32’s auditor use case relies on exactly that.

An extended key travels as 78 bytes: a version, the depth in the tree, the parent’s fingerprint, the child number, the chain code and the key. Base58Check adds four checksum bytes and produces exactly 111 characters, beginning `xpub` or `xprv` on mainnet.

blocks.title: One node, two serializations
blocks.caption: Only the version and the key data differ. Depth, parent fingerprint, child number and chain code are identical: they describe the node’s place in the tree, and the chain code is shared by both forms. The checksum differs only as a consequence.

blocks.text: The fingerprint is the first four bytes of the Hash160 of a key’s public key. It only helps software spot parents and children quickly. Different keys can share a fingerprint, and BIP 32 says software must be willing to deal with such collisions.

blocks.summary: Checks when importing an extended public key

blocks.text: Importing an extended public key also requires a check that its X coordinate corresponds to a point on the curve. BIP 32’s fifth test vector is a list of malformed keys of this and other kinds, and the decoder behind this page rejects all sixteen of them, each for its stated reason.

sections.heading: A tree, not a wallet layout

blocks.text: BIP 32 suggests accounts as hardened children of the master, each with an external chain for receiving and an internal chain for change: m/iH/0/k and m/iH/1/k. It explicitly allows other layouts. Later path conventions build on the same derivation mechanism, so an unfamiliar path does not by itself mean a wallet is broken.

BIP 32 asks for a seed of 128 to 512 bits from a random number generator, and advises 256. The 64-byte seed that BIP 39 produces, described in the previous chapter, fits. The BIP 39 test vector file referenced by BIP 39 also lists the master extended key for each of its 24 English seeds, and the tests behind this page reproduce all of them.

From that one value, every node can have 2³¹ normal and 2³¹ hardened children, and every one of them can be recomputed from the seed alone. That is the whole promise of the title: a single backup covers the entire tree.
